messages.subject: group / cluster size from dht2()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Distance Group,

I've MCDS modelled spatially replicated surveys to derive density using dht2(). Observations are of clusters and I beleive the dht2() output also describes clusters. I would like help to derive average cluster size so that I can get an abundance estimate for individuals (if this is possible in a replicate scenario)?

Below is an example of my flatfiling and dht2'ing and fro'ing.

# make a flatfile useful for dht2 to model MCDS
flatfile.mcds <- data.frame(object = front.data$object, distance = front.data$distance, Sample.Label = front.data$Sample.Label,
                          Region.Label = front.data$Region.Label, Rep = front.data$replicate)

flatfile.mcds <- left_join(flatfile.mcds, region.data)
flatfile.mcds <- left_join(flatfile.mcds, final.samples)

# make a covariate data frame to join to flatfile
mcds.covars <- data.frame(object = front.data$object, obsname = front.data$obsname, side = front.data$side)

# Now join covariates to flatfile using object.
flatfile.mcds <- left_join(flatfile.mcds, mcds.covars)

# Compute abundance estimates over FG, "Flats" Region.

FG.roo.MCDS <- dht2(ddf = MCDS.25,
                        flatfile = flatfile.mcds,
                        stratification = "effort_sum",
                        strat_formula = ~Rep,
                        ci_width = 0.95)
FG.roo.MCDS

Thank you,
Evan

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] group / cluster size from dht2()
messages.body_plain:
Evan

Good to hear from you again.

I have to confess, I've not used dht2​ with objects that occur in groups. However, I altered one of the data sets that ships with the Distance package minke​ to create a size​ field. After fitting a detection function and using dht2​, I printed the resulting object summary. The estimates produced by dht2​ are for numbers of individuals, not numbers of groups. Average group size and variability in group size is also generated in the output.  This appears to hold regardless of the value of the stratification​ argument to dht2.  See below.

library(Distance)
data(minke)
library(dsims)
minke$size <- dsims:::rztpois(dim(minke)[1], 2)  # manufacture a group size
minke.trunc <- 1.5
minke.df.all <- ds(minke, truncation=minke.trunc, key="hr", adjustment=NULL)
summary(minke.df.all)
usingdht2 <- dht2(ddf=minke.df.all, flatfile=minke,
                  strat_formula=~Region.Label, stratification="geographical")
print(usingdht2)

minke$Area <- minke$Area[1]
minke.df.all <- ds(minke, truncation=minke.trunc, key="hr", adjustment=NULL)
summary(minke.df.all)
test <- dht2(ddf=minke.df.all, flatfile=minke,
             strat_formula=~Region.Label, stratification="replicate")
print(test)

I'm not sure using effort_sum​ is the best form of the stratification argument, if your surveys are replicates, then specify replicate​ as the value of the argument.  Hope that helps.

Hi Eric

😂 I think I'll put 'ddf ninja' on my resume - although after reading this it may become apparent I'm only on my yellow belt!

I've described the study to you incorrectly, very sorry but I've sent you down the wrong path here. I said it was 'spatially' replicated but I think the samples should be treated as temporally replicated. We sampled the same study region 11 times over 3 days with a coverage of ~ 20% for each replicate. This is why I'd specified the "effort_sum" stratification argument. The alternative argument "replicate" gives the same abundance estimate

I had some trouble recreating the situation witht the minke example you sent. So I've included my model for you to reference instead.

Just to recap my problem - I suspect dht2() is giving me an estimate for groups rather than individuals in this particular situation. It may be related to temporal stratification.

# AIC chosen model
MCDS.25 <- ddf(data=front.data, dsmodel = ~mcds(key="hn", formula = ~side+obsname),
     meta.data=list(binned=TRUE,point=FALSE,width=300,breaks=c(0,50,100,200,300))

# make a flatfile useful for dht2 to model MCDS
flatfile.mcds <- data.frame(object = front.data$object, distance = front.data$distance, Sample.Label = front.data$Sample.Label,
                          Region.Label = front.data$Region.Label, Rep = front.data$replicate)

flatfile.mcds <- left_join(flatfile.mcds, final.samples)

# make a covariate data frame to join to flatfile

# Now join covariates to flatfile using object.
flatfile.mcds <- left_join(flatfile.mcds, mcds.covars)

# Compute abundance estimates over FG, "Flats" Region.

FG.roo.MCDS <- dht2(ddf = MCDS.25,
                        flatfile = flatfile.mcds,
                        stratification = "effort_sum",
                        strat_formula = ~Rep,
                        ci_width = 0.95)

Hello,

Currently, I am estimating variation in density of Gopher Tortoises across various habitats at a large study site. Separate surveys were designed and analyzed for each habitat type (scrub, pine, prairie) using Distance software. I would like to manually calculate the global density and confidence interval for the entire site, but I'm having a hard time tracking down the appropriate formulas. I have included some details about the models in question.

The scrub model was not stratified.
The pine model was stratified by pine flatwoods and pine plantations.
The prairie model was a cluster analysis of detected burrows with mean cluster size corresponding the the occupancy rate to convert burrows to tortoises. This model was also stratified by dry and mesic prairies.

Could you please point me in the right direction?

Best,
Kammie

Good day,

When the difference in point estimates from dht2 and bootdht are large as in Verity's case, the confidence interval reported by bootdht may not be useful because it's centered on the boostrap mean. Similarly, the magnitude of the bootdht SE is affected by the magnitude of the bootdht mean estimate. However, one can calculate a new symmetrical or (preferably) log-normal confidence interval from the dht2 point estimate and the CV reported by bootdht. The bootstrap CV (0.29) is larger than the analytic CV (0.215) so will inflate the confidence interval and avoid potential underestimation of variance by the analytical method (due to potentially severe overdispersion) as intended.

Eric R, please correct me if this is wrong:
Calculate an SE around the dht2 point estimate as:
dht2 Estimate * bootdht CV, so
2.466 * 0.29 = 0.714; this is larger than the analytic SE (avoids underestimation of variance) but smaller than the SE around the higher bootdht estimate (because it's scaled to the smaller dht2 point estimate).

Now you have an SE appropriate to your dht2 point estimate and your bootstrap precision, and you can calculate log-normal confidence limits following the Buckland et al. distance sampling books, e.g. Buckland et al. (2001) p. 77, or Buckland et al. (2015) p. 107

-e

My query has been solved so I am posting the soltuion here in case it's of use to anyone.

In this example, enquring about the appropriate results to report led to another question: why I have such different results from the point estimate producted by dht2 and the results of the bootstrap - specifically, the confidence interval bounds provided by the bootstrap did not include the point estimate produced by my actual analysis.  Furthermore, the median of the bootstrap replicate estimates (4.23) was nearly twice the estimate produced by the original analysis (2.46).

This was caused by a misunderstanding of how to include the activity parameter. When fitting the activity model, I limited the data to night time observations (for a nocurnal species). This meant I had only estimated the activity level at night, not over the whole period cameras were operational. For more info:

Cameras always operate 24 hours per day, but the time interval during which you estimate activity should match the daily survey duration used to define the survey duration component of effort (T sub k). The activity analysis was bounded (6 p.m. to 8 a.m.), so you estimated the proportion of the 14-hour nighttime that animals were active, which would be high, and not representative of the proportion of time they are active over a 24 hour day. You might have effectively told the software that animals were active for 50.4% of the entire 24-hour day, when really they're only active for 50.4% of your 14 hour interval.  This would cause overestimation of activity level/temporal effort (I think by a factor of 24/14 or 1.714), and proportional underestimation of density.

Removing the bounds and fitting the model to data from the 24h activity cycle fixed the issue. My results are now:

Results from dht2:

Estimate    se        cv       LCI       UCI        df

4.4396       0.739  0.166  3.2045  6.1509   187.619

Results from bootdht :

median  mean   se      lcl       ucl     cv

4.83       4.89     0.83   3.47   6.74   0.17

And it is now apropriate to report the precision estimates (CI, SE, CV) from `bootdht`.

Thanks to Eric R and Eric H for your help!

Hi Eric,

Dht ninja here. Just reviewed this conversation from a year ago and checking whether there were any updates re variance component analysis?

I think I've managed to extract the component variances for CDS, MCDS and MRDS (likelihoods all estimated in dht()) using a pretty simple function that works for mentioned model types. In the example below, my dht() object is FG.roo.CDS.hn.dht

comvar.er <http://comvar.er/> <- function(a) {
  ComVar.er <- ((a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["er"]]/
                  a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["total"]]) * 100)
  return(ComVar.er)
}

comvar.er <http://comvar.er/>(FG.roo.CDS.hn.dht)

and

comvar.f0 <- function(a) {
  ComVar.f0 <- ((a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["detection"]][["variance"]]/
                       a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["total"]]) * 100)
  return(ComVar.f0)
}

comvar.f0(FG.roo.CDS.hn.dht)

I haven't used this approach before so was just after some validation / any suggestions for efficiency gains (I assume a call for this function is already written into the Distance package).

FYI the data is the same for each model (except MR has 2 observers) and I'm looking at how adding complexity affects bias and precision. The relative contribution of the detection function to total variance appears to be increasing as more complex models account for sources of variance like observer and aircraft speed. This is what I think is happening as the encounter rate doesn't change  because the data is the same - unless the MR model affects encounter rate.

Cheers,
Evan

The method I used in the previous comment appears to work when calculating manually using delta method (see table below). Density CV^2 = ER.CV <http://ER.CV>^2 + DProb.CV^2

edit:  Just to clarify my 'FYI' comment above. Encounter Rate CV remains stable despite an increase in ER in the MRDS model. The detection probability's proportional contribution to the density estimate cv increases with model complexity - this should be expected. The important thing here is the tradeoff between increasing model complexity and reduction in bias

Cheers,
Evan

>   ComVar.er <- ((a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["er"]]/
>                   a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["total"]]) * 100)
>   return(ComVar.er)
> }
>
> comvar.er <http://comvar.er/>(FG.roo.CDS.hn.dht)
>
> and

>   ComVar.f0 <- ((a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["detection"]][["variance"]]/
>                        a[["clusters"]][["vc"]][["total"]]) * 100)
>   return(ComVar.f0)
> }
>

>

Robin

Welcome to the group.

Figuring out the effort associated with camera trapping is not simple, so don't be surprised if it baffles you.

I have broken down the calculation of effort for Howe et al.'s (2017) Maxwells duiker study that used motion sensor-triggered still photographs. The definition of a "snapshot moment" is key; it is the length of time for a camera and sensor to recycle to be ready to take another photo. For the equipment in Howe et al. (2017) that length of time was two seconds. The link below determines the number of those two-second "moments" for the cameras operating during the daily "peak activity period" of the animals over the ~3 month duration of the deployment.
https://erex.github.io/Oct-Quarto/announce/2023-01-15-cameraeffort/index.html

I can't give you a good answer to the definition of a "snapshot moment" when using other camera configurations. Perhaps others on the list may have experience with this.

An ancillary issue is field of view of your cameras/sensors. That also influences the definition of effort. The proportion of a circle "seen" by the cameras can be incorporated into the computation of effort, as done by Howe et al. (2017):

> A camera trap (CT) is deployed at a point k that is independent of animal density for a period of time Tk and set to record images for as long as an animal is present to trigger it. We predetermine a finite set of snapshot moments within Tk, t units of time apart, at which an image of an animal could be obtained. Temporal effort at the point is then Tk/t.
